cards.question: Explain why a metal can remain bonded when layers of metal centres change position.
cards.answer: The centres remain attracted to the delocalised electron population. The bonding is not confined to fixed directional links between selected atom pairs.

cards.question: Identify the charge carriers responsible for electrical conduction in solid copper.
cards.answer: Delocalised electrons moving through the metallic structure.

cards.question: Draw a metallic model showing positive centres and the particles that can carry current.
cards.answer:
Label positive metal centres and mobile delocalised electrons; the arrow represents net electron movement, not migration of the entire solid lattice.

Positive metal centres surrounded by delocalised electrons. Electrons can carry current and attraction can persist when layers shift. Schematic, not a literal electron photograph.

cards.question: Identify a structural difference between diamond and C60.
cards.answer: Diamond is an extended covalent network; C60 consists of discrete covalent cages with weaker attractions between separate cages.

cards.question: Draw a labelled two-dimensional slice of an ionic crystal, making clear what the symbols represent.
cards.answer:
The alternating signs represent positive and negative ions in an extended lattice; the drawing does not represent separate NaCl molecules.

Alternating positive and negative ions in an extended crystal. The drawing is a two-dimensional slice, not a complete three-dimensional lattice or a collection of molecules.

cards.question: Identify what must be weakened when a simple molecular liquid changes into its vapour.
cards.answer: Attractions between whole molecules; the internal covalent framework can remain unchanged.

cards.question: Draw a particle diagram showing why iodine can vaporise while retaining I2 molecules.
cards.answer:
Keep the internal I–I bonds in each pair and increase spacing between separate pairs; the dotted between-molecule interaction is weakened.

Pairs of iodine atoms remain joined within I2 molecules as the molecules move farther apart. Dotted lines represent between-molecule attractions, not the covalent I–I bonds.

cards.question: Identify why graphite can conduct electricity while diamond generally does not in the basic structural model.
cards.answer: Graphite has mobile delocalised electrons associated with its extended sheets; diamond lacks the same mobile electron population in its localised covalent-bond model.

cards.question: Draw a model that could explain a deformable solid conducting through mobile electrons. Label the carrier and the cohesive attraction.
cards.answer:
Use a metallic model: delocalised electrons carry charge and attract the positive centres. Movement of layers need not remove that attraction.

Positive metal centres surrounded by delocalised electrons. Electrons can carry current and attraction can persist when layers shift. Schematic, not a literal electron photograph.

cards.question: Identify a plausible structure for a brittle solid that does not conduct until it melts, when it becomes a good conductor.
cards.answer: An ionic lattice, with fixed ions in the solid and mobile ions in the liquid.

cards.question: Draw the ionic structural model supported by high melting temperature, brittle behaviour and conduction only after melting.
cards.answer:
Use oppositely charged ions in a repeating lattice. Strong attraction accounts for the heating requirement, and melting permits ions to move.

Alternating positive and negative ions in an extended crystal. The drawing is a two-dimensional slice, not a complete three-dimensional lattice or a collection of molecules.

cards.question: State one ideal-gas assumption about particle size. [1]
cards.answer: The volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the volume occupied by the gas. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Suggest what happens to the total kinetic energy of two ideal-gas particles during a collision in a thermally insulated vessel. [1]
cards.answer: It is conserved because the collision is elastic; energy may be transferred between the two particles. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Describe three features of a real-gas sample that allow ideal behaviour to be a useful approximation. [3]
cards.answer: Low pressure leaves particles widely separated [1], so their own volume is negligible relative to the sample volume [1]; high temperature makes average kinetic energy large relative to intermolecular attractions [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Explain why finite molecular size causes deviation from ideal behaviour at very high pressure. [2]
cards.answer: Compression makes molecular volume a significant fraction of the total volume [1], because particles have finite size, so the space available for their motion is less than the ideal model assumes [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: State the general ideal-gas equation. [1]
cards.answer: pV = nRT. [1] Here p is absolute pressure in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, T in K and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Calculate the amount of an ideal gas occupying 1.80 dm³ at 125 kPa and 300 K. Use R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and report three significant figures. [3]
cards.answer: n = pV/(RT). Conversion: p = 125000 Pa, V = 1.80 × 10⁻³ m³ [1]. Substitution: n = 125000 × 1.80 × 10⁻³/(8.31 × 300) [1]. Answer: 0.0903 mol to three significant figures [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Determine the volume when the absolute pressure of a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant temperature changes from 100 kPa to 200 kPa. Its initial volume is 4.00 dm³. [1]
cards.answer: 2.00 dm³ [1]: the pressure doubles, so the volume halves because pV is constant for fixed amount and temperature.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

cards.question: Describe an exothermic reaction in terms of heat transfer, product enthalpy and the sign of ΔH. [3]
cards.answer: Heat is transferred from the reacting system to its surroundings [1]; products have lower enthalpy than reactants [1]; ΔH is negative [1].

cards.question: Explain why a solution surrounding an exothermic reaction can warm while the reaction has negative ΔH. [2]
cards.answer: The reaction loses energy as heat, so its enthalpy change is negative [1]; because the solution gains this heat, its temperature rises [1].

cards.question: Describe standard enthalpy change of formation using its amount basis, starting materials and reference states. [3]
cards.answer: It forms one mole of compound [1] from its constituent elements [1] in their standard states at standard pressure and a specified temperature [1].

cards.question: Explain why Cl2(g) → 2Cl(g) is a bond-dissociation equation but is twice the atomisation equation for chlorine. [2]
cards.answer: It breaks one mole of Cl–Cl bonds [1]; atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms, so its equation is ½Cl2(g) → Cl(g) [1].

cards.question: State the equation linking reaction heat to solution mass m, specific heat capacity c and temperature rise ΔT, assuming negligible heat transfer elsewhere. [1]
cards.answer: qreaction = −mcΔT [1]. Molar ΔH requires dividing this sample heat by the relevant amount of reaction.

cards.question: Calculate the molar enthalpy of neutralisation when 0.0250 mol water forms and 60.0 g solution warms by 5.00 K. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect other heat transfers. Give three significant figures. [3]
cards.answer: qsolution = mcΔT = 60.0 × 4.18 × 5.00 = 1254 J [1]. Convert qreaction = −1.254 kJ and use ΔH = qreaction/n [1]. Answer: −1.254/0.0250 = −50.2 kJ mol⁻¹ to three significant figures [1].

cards.question: Determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic when it cools its surrounding solution by 3.0 K, assuming no other heat transfers. [1]
cards.answer: Endothermic [1]: the solution loses heat, so the reaction absorbs it.

cards.question: Describe the energy transfers in breaking reactant bonds, forming product bonds and obtaining an exothermic net change. [3]
cards.answer: Breaking bonds requires energy [1]; forming bonds releases energy [1]; an exothermic net change occurs when formation releases more energy than breaking requires [1].

cards.question: Explain why breaking bonds alone cannot account for the net heat released by combustion. [2]
cards.answer: Breaking bonds requires an energy input [1]; because forming product bonds releases more energy than the input in an exothermic combustion, the overall change releases heat [1].

cards.question: State the bond-energy relationship used to estimate a gaseous reaction enthalpy. [1]
cards.answer: ΔH ≈ ΣE(bonds broken) − ΣE(bonds formed) [1], with bond counts taken from the balanced equation.

cards.question: Calculate ΔH for H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g) using bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243 and H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹. [3]
cards.answer: Input = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ [1]; output magnitude = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ [1]; ΔH ≈ 679 − 864 = −185 kJ mol⁻¹ for the equation as written [1]. No unit conversion is needed. Whole-kJ precision follows the supplied whole-number bond data.

cards.question: Determine whether a gaseous reaction is exothermic or endothermic if breaking its reactant bonds requires 700 kJ and forming its product bonds releases 820 kJ on the same reaction basis. [1]
cards.answer: Exothermic [1], because the release on forming bonds exceeds the energy input.

cards.question: State one reason a mean-bond-enthalpy estimate can differ from a specific reaction enthalpy for the same gaseous endpoints. [1]
cards.answer: Mean bond enthalpies average over molecular environments, so they may differ from the actual values for the particular molecules [1].

cards.question: Calculate the percentage discrepancy of a mean-bond estimate of −190 kJ mol⁻¹ from a specific value of −204 kJ mol⁻¹ for identical gaseous endpoints. Use the magnitude of the specific value as denominator and give two significant figures. [3]
cards.answer: Relationship: percentage discrepancy = |estimate − reference|/|reference| × 100. Difference = |−190 − (−204)| = 14 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]. Substitution = 14/204 × 100 = 6.8627 percent [1]. Answer: 6.9% to two significant figures [1]; the common energy units cancel, so no conversion is required.

cards.question: Determine which comparison requires a phase-change correction: A two values for identical gaseous endpoints; B a gaseous-water bond estimate and a liquid-water combustion value. [1]
cards.answer: B [1]: the water states differ, so a phase-change term is needed before the values describe matching endpoints.

cards.question: State Hess’s law. [1]
cards.answer: The enthalpy change between given initial and final states is independent of the route taken [1].

cards.question: Calculate ΔH for B → C when the same-basis changes A → C and A → B are −120 and −45 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. [3]
cards.answer: Hess relationship: ΔH(A → C) = ΔH(A → B) + ΔH(B → C) [1]. Substitute −120 = −45 + x [1]. Answer x = −75 kJ mol⁻¹ [1], to the nearest kJ as supplied; no unit conversion is needed.

cards.question: Determine the sign change required when a thermochemical equation is reversed to fit a Hess cycle. [1]
cards.answer: Reverse the sign of its ΔH [1], because initial and final states exchange places.

cards.question: State the common final substances used to combine standard combustion data for C(s, graphite), H2(g) and CH4(g) into a methane formation cycle with liquid water. [1]
cards.answer: CO2(g) and H2O(l), in matching amounts on both routes [1].

cards.question: Calculate ΔH°f(CH4) from combustion values C(s, graphite): −394; H2(g): −286; CH4(g): −890 kJ mol⁻¹, with matching CO2(g) and H2O(l) endpoints. [3]
cards.answer: Relationship ΔH°f(CH4) = ΔH°c(C) + 2ΔH°c(H2) − ΔH°c(CH4) [1]. Substitution −394 + 2(−286) − (−890) [1]. Answer −76 kJ mol⁻¹ [1], to the nearest kJ as supplied. No unit conversion is required.

cards.question: Determine why combustion enthalpies cannot be combined directly in a formation cycle if one route ends with liquid water and the other ends with steam. [1]
cards.answer: The routes have different final states [1]; include a phase-change enthalpy to make their endpoints match.

cards.question: State what the vertical and horizontal axes represent in a reaction pathway diagram. [1]
cards.answer: Vertical: enthalpy; horizontal: progress of reaction [1].

cards.question:
Determine ΔH from this reaction pathway diagram. Then sketch the same profile and label the forward activation-energy interval as additional practice. [1]

Energy profile: vertical axis enthalpy / kJ mol⁻¹; horizontal reaction progress. Reactants at 0, transition peak at +80, products at −40. Forward activation energy 80 kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change −40 kJ mol⁻¹; reverse activation energy 120 kJ mol⁻¹. Solution information belongs on answer side when assessing these quantities.
cards.answer: ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹ [1], because products lie 40 kJ mol⁻¹ below reactants. In the practice sketch, label enthalpy and progress axes, reactants and products, and the activation interval from reactants to the peak (80 kJ mol⁻¹).

cards.question: State the sum of oxidation numbers for the atoms in a polyatomic ion. [1]
cards.answer: It equals the overall charge on that ion [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in Cr2O7²−, taking oxygen as −2. Show the charge sum. [3]
cards.answer: Charge-sum equation: 2x + 7(−2) = −2 [1]. Thus 2x = +12 [1] and each chromium is +6 [1]. The result is exact and dimensionless; conversion and significant-figure rounding are inapplicable.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Determine whether nitrogen is oxidised or reduced when its oxidation number changes from +3 to +5. [1]
cards.answer: Oxidised [1], because its oxidation number increases.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Describe zinc and copper(II) ions in Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), giving electron transfer and the oxidising agent. [3]
cards.answer: Zinc loses two electrons and is oxidised [1]; Cu2+ gains two electrons and is reduced [1]; Cu2+ is the oxidising agent [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Explain why Fe2+ is a reducing agent when it becomes Fe3+. [2]
cards.answer: Fe2+ loses an electron and is oxidised [1]; because another species accepts that electron and is reduced, Fe2+ acts as the reducing agent [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: State the electron-balance requirement used when balancing a redox equation. [1]
cards.answer: Total electrons lost equal total electrons gained [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Write the balanced ionic equation for MnO4− reacting with Fe2+ in acidic aqueous solution to form Mn2+ and Fe3+. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: MnO4−(aq) + 8H+(aq) + 5Fe2+(aq) → Mn2+(aq) + 4H2O(l) + 5Fe3+(aq). Correct species and acidic H+/water balance [1]; electron ratio and overall charge/atom balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: State the colour change when an oxidising sample liberates iodine from colourless aqueous potassium iodide. [1]
cards.answer: Colourless to brown [1], as iodine forms.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Suggest the redox role of a sample that decolourises purple potassium manganate(VII) acidified with dilute sulphuric acid. [1]
cards.answer: It acts as a reducing agent [1], reducing Mn(VII) to Mn(II).
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Name NO3− using the syllabus oxidation-number convention. [1]
cards.answer: Nitrate(V) [1]; nitrogen is +5.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Suggest the syllabus oxyanion name for ClO−, in which chlorine has oxidation number +1. [1]
cards.answer: Chlorate(I) [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: Explain the error in naming NO2− nitrate(V), using an oxidation-number calculation as a discriminating test. [2]
cards.answer: The V wrongly assigns nitrogen +5 [1]. Charge balance gives x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3 and the correct name is nitrate(III) [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

cards.question: State what electrolysis does to a suitable electrolyte. [1]
cards.answer: Passing an electric current through it causes chemical decomposition [1].

cards.question: Suggest why molten sodium chloride conducts by ion movement but solid sodium chloride does not. [1]
cards.answer: Its ions can move in the melt, whereas the ions in the solid lattice are fixed [1].

cards.question: State the cathode product expected from dilute aqueous copper(II) sulphate with inert electrodes in the ordinary school selective-discharge model. [1]
cards.answer: Copper metal [1].

cards.question: Suggest the anode gas from concentrated aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes. [1]
cards.answer: Chlorine [1]; concentrated chloride favours chloride discharge in this cell.

cards.question: State the electrode at which copper ions are reduced when copper is recovered electrolytically from a prepared acidic leach solution. [1]
cards.answer: The cathode [1].

cards.question: Suggest the chemical reason for a growing copper deposit on the cathode during recovery from a prepared copper(II) leach solution. [1]
cards.answer: Cu2+ ions gain electrons to form Cu(s) on the cathode [1].

cards.question: State which side of a cathode reduction half-equation contains the electrons. [1]
cards.answer: The reactant, left-hand side [1].

cards.question: Write the anode half-equation for chlorine formation from concentrated aqueous chloride with an inert anode. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: 2Cl−(aq) → Cl2(g) + 2e−. Correct reactant/product and states [1]; atom and charge balance including electrons [1].

cards.question: State the charge carriers in the metallic wires and in the liquid electrolyte of an electrolytic circuit. [1]
cards.answer: Electrons in the wires; mobile ions in the electrolyte [1].

cards.question: Suggest why a claim that free electrons travel through the bulk aqueous electrolyte from cathode to anode is incorrect. [1]
cards.answer: Ions carry charge through the electrolyte; electron transfer occurs at the electrode interfaces [1].

cards.question: Describe dynamic equilibrium in a closed reaction system at constant temperature, in terms of continuing reactions, rates and concentrations. [3]
cards.answer: Forward and reverse reactions continue [1] at equal rates [1], so reactant and product concentrations remain constant [1].

cards.question: Explain why constant concentrations in a closed system at fixed temperature do not mean the forward and reverse reactions have stopped at dynamic equilibrium. [2]
cards.answer: The two reactions continue at equal rates [1]; because species are made and consumed at matching rates, there is no net concentration change [1].

cards.question: State Le Chatelier’s principle for a system subjected to a change in temperature, pressure or concentration. [1]
cards.answer: The equilibrium system responds in a direction that tends to oppose the imposed temperature, pressure or concentration change [1].

cards.question: Determine the favoured direction for N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) when pressure rises by compression at constant temperature. [1]
cards.answer: Towards ammonia [1], because that side contains fewer gaseous particles.

cards.question: State which of temperature, concentration, pressure or catalyst can change the equilibrium constant for a specified reaction. [1]
cards.answer: Temperature [1]; the other changes do not change K at fixed temperature.

cards.question: Suggest the effect on Kc when a catalyst is added at the same temperature to a reversible mixture. [1]
cards.answer: No change [1]; equilibrium is reached faster but the constant at that temperature is unchanged.

cards.question: State what supplies the powers in a Kc expression written using equilibrium concentrations. [1]
cards.answer: The stoichiometric coefficients in the balanced equation [1].

cards.question: Determine the Kp expression for 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) at a stated temperature. [1]
cards.answer: Kp = p(SO3)²/(p(SO2)²p(O2)) [1], using equilibrium partial pressures.

cards.question: State which concentrations must be used when calculating Kc at a stated temperature. [1]
cards.answer: Equilibrium concentrations [1], rather than unadjusted initial values.

cards.question: Calculate Kc for H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at a stated temperature using equilibrium concentrations [H2] = [I2] = 0.200 and [HI] = 0.800 mol dm⁻³. Give three significant figures. [3]
cards.answer: Relationship Kc = [HI]²/([H2][I2]) [1]. Substitution 0.800²/(0.200 × 0.200) [1]. Answer 16.0, dimensionless in this concentration convention, to three significant figures [1]. Concentration units cancel; no conversion is needed.

cards.question: Determine whether a large Kc by itself shows a fast reaction at the stated temperature. [1]
cards.answer: No [1]: Kc concerns equilibrium concentration ratios, whereas rate requires kinetic information.

cards.question: State the stoichiometric rule for concentration changes in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 at fixed volume. [1]
cards.answer: A decrease of x in nitrogen concentration accompanies a decrease of 3x in hydrogen and an increase of 2x in ammonia [1].

cards.question: Calculate final moles of B for the model A(aq) ⇌ B(aq), Kc = 4.00 at the stated temperature, initially 1.00 mol A and no B in 1.00 dm³. [3]
cards.answer: Let x mol B form: final A = 1.00 − x and B = x [1]. Kc = x/(1.00 − x) = 4.00 gives 5.00x = 4.00 [1]. Answer x = 0.800 mol B to three significant figures [1]. Equal volume factors cancel; no conversion is required.

cards.question: Determine whether a proposed equilibrium calculation giving a negative final reactant concentration can be physically accepted. [1]
cards.answer: No [1]; a final amount or concentration must be non-negative, so the model setup or chosen result needs correction.

cards.question: Describe the temperature, pressure and catalyst reasoning for the exothermic Haber reaction N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. [3]
cards.answer: Lower temperature favours equilibrium ammonia but slows rate, requiring a compromise [1]; higher pressure favours the fewer gas particles on the ammonia side but has costs [1]; a suitable catalyst increases rate without changing equilibrium yield at fixed temperature [1].

cards.question: Explain why a catalyst does not replace the temperature compromise in an exothermic industrial equilibrium process. [2]
cards.answer: At a chosen temperature it speeds approach but does not change the equilibrium yield [1]; because higher temperature generally improves rate while lowering the attainable product yield, both effects still matter [1].

cards.question: Explain why “the lowest temperature must be best because it gives most ammonia” is incomplete for the exothermic Haber process. [2]
cards.answer: It considers equilibrium yield but omits rate [1]; low temperature favours ammonia yet slows production, so a practical temperature balances yield and rate [1].

cards.question: State two types of data needed to distinguish equilibrium conversion from productivity at a stated temperature and pressure. [1]
cards.answer: Equilibrium conversion or composition and a rate or output-per-time measurement [1].

cards.question: Determine which setting gives greater output per minute for a model exothermic process: at the same pressure and feed, cooler gives 80% equilibrium conversion and 2.0 mol min⁻¹, warmer gives 60% and 5.0 mol min⁻¹. The sole criterion is output per minute. [1]
cards.answer: The warmer setting [1], because 5.0 mol min⁻¹ exceeds 2.0 mol min⁻¹ despite its lower conversion.

cards.question: Describe a Brønsted–Lowry acid, a base and the relationship between a conjugate pair. [3]
cards.answer: An acid donates H+ [1]; a base accepts H+ [1]; a conjugate acid–base pair differs by one H+ [1].

cards.question: Explain why NH3 acts as a base in NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq), and name its conjugate acid. [2]
cards.answer: NH3 accepts H+ from water [1], becoming its conjugate acid NH4+ [1].

cards.question: Describe the difference between strong and weak monoprotic acids at the same analytical concentration and temperature. [3]
cards.answer: The strong acid dissociates essentially completely [1], while the weak acid dissociates partly [1]; the strong acid has higher H+ concentration and lower pH [1].

cards.question: Explain why diluting a strong acid does not turn it into a weak acid. [2]
cards.answer: Dilution reduces its concentration, the amount per unit volume [1]; strength concerns extent of dissociation, which remains essentially complete for the stated dilute strong-acid model [1].

cards.question: State the pH relationship using hydrogen-ion concentration for the dilute-solution school model. [1]
cards.answer: pH = −log10[H+] [1], with [H+] entered in mol dm⁻³; pH is dimensionless.

cards.question: Calculate [H+] and pH for 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ HCl, treating it as fully dissociated and neglecting water’s contribution. [3]
cards.answer: [H+] = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ from the one-H+ monoprotic relationship [1]. pH = −log10(0.0200) [1]. Answer 1.699, dimensionless, to three decimal places for the three-significant-figure concentration [1]. No unit conversion is required.

cards.question: Determine which solution has the greater hydrogen-ion concentration: pH 2.00 or pH 3.00. [1]
cards.answer: The pH 2.00 solution [1]; its H+ concentration is ten times greater.

cards.question: Describe a concentration-based reaction rate, its time basis and a suitable unit. [3]
cards.answer: Change in a stated reactant or product concentration [1] per unit time [1], for example mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why a falling reactant concentration gives a positive disappearance rate when written as −Δ[reactant]/Δt. [2]
cards.answer: Consumption makes Δ[reactant] negative [1]; the leading minus sign converts that decrease into the positive disappearance-rate magnitude [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Describe how increasing reactant concentration can increase rate in a simple collision-controlled reaction at constant temperature. [3]
cards.answer: There are more reacting particles per unit volume [1], causing more frequent encounters [1] and more successful collisions per second [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why higher concentration can increase rate without raising particle energy when temperature is fixed. [2]
cards.answer: More particles per unit volume increase collision frequency [1]; the energy distribution is unchanged at fixed temperature, so the increase comes from more encounters [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Describe activation energy and its representation on a Boltzmann distribution, including the meaning of the area beyond it. [3]
cards.answer: Ea is the minimum collision energy required for reaction [1]; it is marked on the energy axis as a threshold [1]; the area beyond it represents particles with sufficient energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why a collision can fail to react even when particles meet. [2]
cards.answer: Its energy may be below the activation threshold [1], or its orientation may be unsuitable for the required rearrangement [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why a reaction-pathway profile is not an answer to a request for a Boltzmann distribution, using the axes as a discriminating test. [2]
cards.answer: A pathway profile has enthalpy versus progress of reaction [1]; a Boltzmann distribution needs particle population per energy interval versus energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain the error in labelling the right-hand area under a Boltzmann curve “activation energy”. [2]
cards.answer: Ea is an energy value on the horizontal axis [1]; the area beyond its threshold represents the number or fraction of particles energetic enough, not an energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Describe three effects relevant to a higher-temperature Boltzmann comparison with the same number of particles and the same pathway. [3]
cards.answer: The curve broadens with a lower peak at higher energy [1]; a greater fraction lies above the fixed Ea [1]; increased average speeds also increase collision frequency in a fixed-density comparison [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why heating usually increases rate, using energy distribution and collisions. Keep concentration and the reaction pathway unchanged. [2]
cards.answer: The fraction above the unchanged Ea increases [1]; faster particles also collide more frequently, increasing successful collisions per second [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

cards.question: Explain why “heating increases rate because collisions are more frequent” is incomplete for an unchanged pathway. [2]
cards.answer: It omits the energy-distribution change [1]: a greater fraction has energy at least Ea, so a greater fraction of encounters can react [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy
